---
title: "A straight line mean"
execute:
  enabled: true
  echo: true
  warning: false

Our discussion of [conditional means](regression-models.qmd) left $m(x)=\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X=x]$ unrestricted. **Simple linear regression** imposes the straight line restriction stated below.

In this application, $Y$ is the [Provo word position mean](regression-models.qmd#provo-word-position-data) of log first fixation durations among readers with a retained positive fixation. The predictor is **modeled cloze surprisal**, the negative base 2 logarithm of the fitted cloze probability defined in that same discussion. The line consequently describes position summaries grouped in passages rather than raw reader trials or the probability of skipping a word.

The response distribution below assumes [independent](../foundations/independence.qmd) rows only when that condition is explicitly stated. Its [variance](../random-variables-and-distributions/variance-and-covariance.qmd) describes response spread around the line, whereas a coefficient [standard error](../statistical-inference/standard-errors.qmd) describes variation of an estimator across repeated samples.

The key separation is between a straight conditional mean and a Gaussian response distribution around that mean. The Provo fit makes both restrictions visible before its slope is interpreted over the observed surprisal range.

Okay. So what information is contained in a straight line? Pick two predictor values one unit apart. A straight line requires the fitted mean to change by the same amount over every such interval. We call this repeated change the **slope**. We call the line's value at $x=0$ the **intercept**. These names describe two features of the mean function before we make any claim about the distribution of responses around it.

$$
m(x)=\beta_0+\beta_1x.
$$

In this equation, $\beta_0$ is the intercept and $\beta_1$ is the slope. Substituting $x=0$ gives $m(0)=\beta_0$. Substituting $x+1$ and subtracting $m(x)$ gives $\beta_1$. The word *simple* means that the model has one predictor. Here *linear* means that the coefficients enter as a weighted sum, which produces a straight conditional mean as a function of this predictor.

## Mean function versus response distribution

This equation restricts a conditional mean. It does not yet say how individual position summaries vary around that mean. For instance, both

$$
Y_i\mid X_i=x_i\sim\mathcal N(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i,\sigma^2)
$$

and a Student-$t$ response centered at $\beta_0+\beta_1x_i$ share the same line but make different tail assumptions. We next use squared loss to fit the line, and conventional finite sample inference later adds independent errors, constant variance, and a normal response. Keeping these pieces separate prevents a plotted line from silently importing a complete probability model.

## Fitting the Provo regression line

We return to the Provo position summaries and center modeled cloze surprisal at its observed mean. Centering makes the intercept correspond to an observed reference point; the derivation under [centering](centering-predictors.qmd) shows why.

The code follows the definitions in order. It first reconstructs surprisal as $-\log_2(p)$, computes the observed mean surprisal, and subtracts that mean from every position. The call to `lm()` then places `mean_log_ffd` to the left of `~` as the response and the centered surprisal to the right as the predictor. Reading an R formula in this left-to-right way will help when we add more predictors.

```{r}
#| label: fit-provo-simple-regression
library(ggplot2)

provo <- read.csv(
  "data/provo/content-word-positions.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
provo$cloze_surprisal_bits <- -log2(provo$OrthoMatchModel)
surprisal_center <- mean(provo$cloze_surprisal_bits)
provo$cloze_surprisal_c <-
  provo$cloze_surprisal_bits - surprisal_center

fit <- lm(mean_log_ffd ~ cloze_surprisal_c, data = provo)
coefficient_table <- coef(summary(fit))

stopifnot(
  nrow(provo) == 1593L,
  length(unique(provo$Text_ID)) == 55L,
  isTRUE(all.equal(mean(provo$cloze_surprisal_c), 0, tolerance = 1e-12))
)

coefficient_table
```

The following two predictions use the observed Provo fit. They hold every aspect of the fitted model fixed while increasing centered surprisal from its observed mean to one bit above that mean.

```{r}
#| label: compare-provo-one-bit-predictions
one_bit_comparison <- data.frame(cloze_surprisal_c = c(0, 1))
one_bit_comparison$fitted_mean_log_ffd <- predict(
  fit,
  newdata = one_bit_comparison
)
one_bit_comparison
```

Subtracting the first fitted value from the second recovers the fitted slope from the coefficient table. The comparison uses two predictor values tied to the observed Provo center rather than invented response values.

The fitted conditional mean is

$$
\widehat m(x_i)
=
\widehat\beta_0+\widehat\beta_1(x_i-\overline x).
$$

At mean modeled cloze surprisal, the fitted mean log first fixation duration is `r sprintf("%.4f", coef(fit)[["(Intercept)"]])`. Each additional bit of modeled cloze surprisal is associated with a change of `r sprintf("%.4f", coef(fit)[["cloze_surprisal_c"]])` log milliseconds in the fitted position mean.

The slope is a contrast between conditional means:

$$
m(x+1)-m(x)
=
\{\beta_0+\beta_1(x+1)\}
-\{\beta_0+\beta_1x\}
=\beta_1.
$$

Thus the intercept locates the line, while the slope gives its change per predictor unit.

```{r}
#| label: plot-provo-simple-regression
#| fig-cap: "Provo positions aggregated across readers and the fitted straight conditional mean."
grid <- data.frame(
  cloze_surprisal_bits = seq(
    min(provo$cloze_surprisal_bits),
    max(provo$cloze_surprisal_bits),
    length.out = 160L
  )
)
grid$cloze_surprisal_c <-
  grid$cloze_surprisal_bits - surprisal_center
grid$fitted <- predict(fit, newdata = grid)

point_opacity <- 0.22
ggplot(provo, aes(cloze_surprisal_bits, mean_log_ffd)) +
  geom_point(color = "grey65", alpha = point_opacity, size = 0.9) +
  geom_line(
    data = grid,
    aes(cloze_surprisal_bits, fitted),
    color = "#2C6E9B",
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Modeled cloze surprisal (bits)",
    y = "Mean log first fixation duration"
  ) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

The line summarizes an average association across item positions. A potential worry is that the plotted cloud contains nested passages. That concern is well founded: ordinary standard errors do not represent passage clustering, and reader clustering cannot be recovered from this table. We address the remaining passage identifier when deriving [regression uncertainty](linear-regression-uncertainty.qmd).

## Recap and check your understanding

1. Which conditional means are compared by the slope?
2. Why does a one-bit increase have the same fitted change everywhere on the line?
3. Does the positive slope show that surprisal causes longer fixations?
4. Which dependence structure remains visible in the table?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. The slope compares $m(x+1)$ with $m(x)$: fitted mean log FFD at predictor values one bit apart. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. The straight-line restriction makes $m(x+1)-m(x)=\beta_1$ for every $x$. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. No. The slope describes an observational association across item positions and does not identify a causal effect of surprisal. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. Passage membership remains visible through `Text_ID`; reader dependence cannot be recovered after aggregation. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->

</details>

We next use [centering](centering-predictors.qmd) to change the reference point without changing the fitted relation.
